message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core is lightweight and shares resources. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Very simple instruction set, often SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – same operation applied to many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Execution Model** | Serial or lightly parallel – one thread runs at a time per core, but can switch quickly between many threads. | Massive parallelism – thousands of threads run concurrently on many cores. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, sophisticated prefetching. | Smaller per‑core caches, relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory pools. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control‑heavy tasks, branching, I/O, small data sets, latency‑sensitive operations. | Data‑parallel tasks, matrix/vector operations, image/video processing, deep‑learning inference/training. |
| **Power & Heat** | Designed for low power per core, but overall power scales with number of cores. | High throughput per watt; GPUs consume more power but deliver far more FLOPs per watt for parallel workloads. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded programming with standard languages (C/C++, Java, etc.). | Parallel programming frameworks (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, DirectCompute, Metal, etc.) or high‑level APIs (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |

### Bottom line
- **CPU**: “Swiss Army knife” – good at a wide variety of tasks, especially those that require quick decision making and low latency.
- **GPU**: “Specialist” – excels at performing the same operation on many data points at once, delivering huge throughput for tasks that can be parallelized.

In practice, modern systems use both: the CPU handles general system tasks and orchestrates work, while the GPU accelerates heavy‑lifting computations that benefit from parallelism.
